source.title: Scaling Retrieval-Based Language Models with a Trillion-Token Datastore
source.authors: Rulin Shao; Jacqueline He; Akari Asai; Wei-Jia Shi; Tim Dettmers; Sewon Min; Luke S. Zettlemoyer; Pang Wei Koh

page_placements.theme: Retrieval augmentation and datastore scaling shift performance frontiers

record.tranche_reason: The study uses scaling-law and compute-optimal-scaling ideas to analyze retrieval-based LMs, but it studies datastore size as an additional inference-time variable rather than testing the claim's parameter, pretraining-token, or compute laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for datastore scaling and retrieval-augmented models. These results do not test the listed versions' claims about power laws in model parameters, pretraining tokens, or compute, extrapolation from smaller runs, or stable parameter-token allocation. The compute-optimal analysis uses downstream-task performance and includes datastore size as a variable.
record.test_reason: The study scales an inference-time retrieval datastore and borrows the Kaplan/Hoffmann FLOPs approximation (6ND) to build compute-performance curves. It does not fit or check power laws in parameters, pretraining tokens or compute for held-out loss. Its compute-optimal analysis compares retrieval-based and LM-only Pareto frontiers on downstream tasks using released intermediate checkpoints. It does not estimate loss-minimising parameter or token allocations. Datastore scaling is reported as monotone and unsaturated, but no power-law form is fitted, so it does not bear on V5 either.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that larger inference-time datastores monotonically improve language modeling and several downstream tasks, most clearly knowledge-intensive QA. They also find that retrieval-based LMs beat LM-only models at equal training compute, and argue that datastore size should be part of LM efficiency and performance trade-offs.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines retrieval datastore scaling and retrieval-based compute-performance trade-offs; it does not reproduce the original parameter, pretraining-token, or compute loss-scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by task and model capability: benefits are strongest on factual question answering, mixed on MedQA, and weak for Pythia on reasoning-intensive tasks. The paper also reports that reranking and decontamination choices affect results.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing inference-time datastore size lowers perplexity on RedPajama and S2ORC monotonically without saturation, up to 1.4T tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Retrieval datastore size is an additional scaling axis: perplexity of retrieval-augmented LMs falls monotonically with datastore size.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream gains from datastore scaling are large on factual QA, smaller on MMLU, mixed on MedQA, and near nil for weak models on reasoning tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefits of inference-time datastore scaling depend on task type and reader-model capability.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal training FLOPs, retrieval-based Pythia/OLMo models lie above LM-only Pareto frontiers on downstream tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Counting datastore construction as training compute, retrieval-based LMs reach better compute-performance trade-offs than LM-only models.

record.problems: The compute-optimal study uses released intermediate checkpoints rather than newly trained runs; the authors note these checkpoints may underperform what could be achieved at the same compute with different training schedules. The compute-optimal analysis uses downstream-task performance, not held-out loss, and is limited to Pythia and OLMo. The full scaling study uses one retriever. Several per-model results are presented in figures rather than stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted from the per-model datastore-scaling curves in Figures 3 and 9–12, reranker comparisons in Figure 6, or decontamination and filtering ablations in Figures 7 and 13. These concern datastore design or retrieval performance rather than the listed parameter-, token-, or compute-loss claims.

untested.parts: No held-out loss power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute; perplexity is studied only against datastore size.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No estimate of the loss-minimising parameter/token split versus compute; Pareto frontiers use downstream accuracy and existing checkpoints.
Datastore scaling is shown to be monotone, but no power-law form is fitted; no other modality is studied.
LM-only downstream curves against model size and pretraining tokens appear in Figure 4 but are not analysed for predictability.
No comparison of fitting choices or of exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The Figure 4 caption says Pythia models show no meaningful scaling curves on MMLU/MedQA, which might bear on V6. However, the text frames this as a retrieval-benefit result, not an analysis of LM-only predictability with scale, so no V6 row or verdict is given. Compute-optimal curves use intermediate checkpoints sharing one LR schedule, which the authors note may understate attainable performance.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, pretraining tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Whether loss-minimising parameter and token counts follow stable powers of compute, and how their growth rates compare.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from model scale or pretraining loss; the paper varies datastore size and reports downstream results instead.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.
